stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Say "khubz" (bread) and "kitab" (book). Can you feel the rough "kh" sound in your throat?
explain: Arabic has sounds that English does not. "kh" in khubz is a rough sound from the back of the mouth. "q" in qamar (moon) is deeper than "k". "ʿ" in ʿayn (eye) comes from the throat.

Arabic has three short vowels (a, i, u) and three long vowels (ā, ī, ū). Long vowels last twice as long. Small marks above and below the letters, called harakat, show the short vowels. In this level the words are shown with harakat so you can read them.
Arabic words in this course use Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), the shared language of books, news and school. At home, people speak local dialects. We show the word endings in the short, spoken style.
stages.mnemonic: Khubz and kitab: rough "kh" in the throat, soft "k" at the lips.
sentences: The moon is in the sky.

gq.q: Which sound is made in the throat in the word ʿayn (eye)?
o: The letter ك (k) at the front
gq.why: It is a throat sound that has no English letter, so we show it as ʿ.

gq.q: How do long vowels differ from short vowels in Arabic?
o: They last about twice as long
They are written with no letter at all
gq.why: Long vowels are held for about two beats; short vowels are quick.

panel.q: Why does Arabic need the sounds q and k as two different sounds?
o: They change meaning: qalb (heart) and kalb (dog) are different words
Q is a rarer spelling of K that is only found in old poetry
Arabic has no K sound, so q is used for every k
They are two spellings of one sound in different dialects
panel.why: The two sounds make different words, so mixing them changes meaning.

panel.q: Why do beginners see harakat in this course?
o: They show short vowels, which are usually left out in newspapers and books
They show which words are plural or feminine in books
They are decoration that printers add to make a text look formal and old
They show where a question begins in a sentence
panel.why: Short vowels are normally unwritten for adults, so harakat help learners read correctly.

panel.q: Name one Arabic sound that does not exist in English and say which word shows it.
panel.model: The rough kh in khubz (bread), or ʿ in ʿayn (eye), or q in qamar (moon), are not found in English.
panel.why: Arabic has throat and back-of-mouth sounds such as kh, ʿ, ḥ and q.

teach.model: Arabic has sounds like kh in khubz, q in qamar and ʿ in ʿayn. They are made at the back of the mouth or in the throat. Short vowels are shown by small marks called harakat.

points.ask: Which sound is in the word for bread?
What sound starts the word for moon?
What are the small marks on the letters for?

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: This line runs from right to left. Which way do you think your eyes should go?
explain: Arabic is written from right to left. The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters. Most letters join to the next letter, so a letter can look a little different at the start, middle or end of a word.

Six letters do not join to the letter after them: ا (alif), د (dāl), ذ (dhāl), ر (rā), ز (zāy) and و (wāw). Capital letters do not exist. Letters are made from dots and curves; the dots matter: ب has one dot below, ت two above, ث three above.
Today we meet some letter names: alif, bāʾ, tāʾ, jīm, dāl, sīn, mīm, nūn.
stages.mnemonic: Right to left: start at the right, like a door that opens the other way.
sentences: Arabic is written from right to left.

gq.q: How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet?
Which letter has one dot below it?
gq.why: ب (bāʾ) has one dot under it. ت and ن have two and one dot above; ث has three above.

panel.q: Why do dots matter in Arabic writing?
o: Letters with the same shape are told apart by dots, so ب, ت and ث are different
Dots show the end of a sentence, much like a full stop does in English
Dots show long vowels, as the macron does in English
Dots are only decoration and can be left out freely
panel.why: Several letters share a base shape. The number and place of dots decide which letter it is.

panel.q: Which letter never joins to the letter that follows it?
o: ب (bāʾ), which is always written alone
س (sīn), because it has three teeth
م (mīm), because it is a round letter
panel.why: Alif is one of six letters that connect only to the letter before them.

panel.q: A learner sees the same letter written two ways in one word. What is the best explanation?
o: Letters change shape depending on where they are in the word
The word has a spelling mistake and must be corrected
The writer made a spelling mistake and used two fonts
One shape is for boys' names and one for girls' names
panel.why: Arabic letters can have initial, medial, final and separate forms.

teach.model: Arabic is written from right to left with 28 letters. Most letters join together, and the shape changes a little at the start, middle or end of a word. Dots tell similar letters apart.

points.ask: Which way do you read?
How many letters are there?
Why do the letters look different in a word?

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: In Arabic, a very common greeting means "peace be upon you". Why might people greet each other with a wish?
explain: The usual Arabic greeting is as-salāmu ʿalaykum, "peace be upon you". The reply is wa ʿalaykumu s-salām, "and upon you peace". It is used across the Arab world in MSA and in all dialects.
For "good morning" say ṣabāḥ al-khayr. The reply is ṣabāḥ an-nūr, "a morning of light". Many greetings are replied to with a richer wish.

Dialects add their own greetings. In Egypt people often ask "izzayyak?" and in the Levant "kīfak?". Both mean "how are you?", which in MSA is kayfa ḥāluk. In this course we use MSA, unless we name a dialect.
stages.mnemonic: Greeting = wish. Say a wish, and get a better wish back.

gq.q: What is the usual reply to as-salāmu ʿalaykum?
o: ṣabāḥ al-khayr, which means good morning
gq.why: The reply returns the wish: "and upon you peace".

gq.q: Which phrase is MSA for "how are you?" (to a man)?
gq.why: Kayfa ḥāluka is MSA. izzayyak is Egyptian, kīfak is Levantine and shlonak is Gulf or Iraqi.

panel.q: Why is "izzayyak" not used in a news broadcast in MSA?
o: It belongs to Egyptian Arabic, a spoken dialect
It is rude in all Arabic and must never be said
It is only used when talking to young children
It is a word borrowed from a different language family
panel.why: News usually uses MSA; dialect forms belong to speech among friends and family.

panel.q: A friend says "ṣabāḥ al-khayr". Which reply sounds most natural?
panel.why: The classic reply is "morning of light". Masāʾ is evening, so it does not fit.

panel.q: Why is it polite to answer a greeting with a fuller wish?
o: It is a custom of generosity: you return a greeting with at least as much good
Because Arabic grammar demands the longer form of every greeting each time
So that the listener can understand you more easily
Because greetings in Arabic are always very short words
panel.why: Replies like "and upon you peace" or "morning of light" return and often increase the wish.

teach.model: Say as-salāmu ʿalaykum, meaning peace be upon you. The answer is wa ʿalaykumu s-salām. For good morning say ṣabāḥ al-khayr and reply ṣabāḥ an-nūr.

points.ask: What does the greeting mean?
What do I say back?
How do I say good morning?

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: Count 1, 2, 3 in your head. Arabic has its own digits too. Do you think they look like ours?
explain: Arabic numbers one to ten are wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arbaʿa, khamsa, sitta, sabʿa, thamāniya, tisʿa, ʿashara. In much of the Arab world, people write ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ ٠, called Eastern Arabic numerals, while the Maghreb often uses 1 2 3.

Numbers are written left to right even inside right-to-left text. The numbers 3 to 10 look backwards in grammar: with a masculine thing the number ends in -a, and with a feminine thing it drops the -a. So "three books" is thalāthat kutub, but "three girls" is thalāth banāt.
Remember that wāḥid (one) and ithnān (two) usually follow the noun and agree with it: kitāb wāḥid, one book.
stages.mnemonic: Number 3 to 10 plays opposite: boy = with a, girl = without.

gq.q: Which digits do many Arab countries, such as Egypt and Saudi Arabia, use for 3 and 5?
gq.why: Eastern Arabic numerals ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩ are widely used in the Middle East.

gq.q: "Five cats": cat is qiṭṭa (feminine). Which is right?
gq.why: With feminine plurals of 3–10 the number drops the -a: khams qiṭaṭ.

panel.q: A teacher says "thalāth banāt" (three girls) and "thalāthat awlād" (three boys). What is the rule?
o: Numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender from the counted noun
The number always agrees with the gender of the noun
The number always agrees in gender with the noun counted
Only masculine nouns can be counted in Arabic
panel.why: Arabic reverses gender with 3–10: feminine nouns get the shorter form, masculine nouns get the form with -a.

panel.q: Why is the number written 3 or ٣ inside an Arabic sentence still read left to right?
o: Digits are written left to right, even in right-to-left text
The number is a picture so it has no direction at all
The number is really a picture, so it has no direction at all
The writer is left-handed and wrote the digit by hand
panel.why: In both numeral systems the digits of a number run left to right.

panel.q: Why can wāḥid (one) be dropped after a noun?
o: The singular noun already means one, so wāḥid adds emphasis
Arabic never counts one, so wāḥid is not a real word at all
One is not a real number in Arabic grammar
It is only used when talking about money or prices
panel.why: kitāb alone means a book; kitāb wāḥid stresses "one single book".

teach.model: Count from one to ten with wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arbaʿa, khamsa, sitta, sabʿa. Arabic has its own digits ١ ٢ ٣. Numbers from three to ten take the opposite gender form from the thing counted.

points.ask: How do I say one and two?
Do the numbers look the same as ours?
What is odd about three to ten?

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: Look around you. If a girl and a boy both have a red ball, would the word for "red" change?
explain: Colours in Arabic are adjectives, so they agree with the noun. For a masculine noun the colour is aḥmar (red); for a feminine noun it is ḥamrāʾ. Other colours work the same way: azraq / zarqāʾ (blue), akhḍar / khaḍrāʾ (green), aṣfar / ṣafrāʾ (yellow), abyaḍ / bayḍāʾ (white), aswad / sawdāʾ (black).
Adjectives come after the noun: tuffāḥa ḥamrāʾ, a red apple. Shapes: dāʾira (circle), murabbaʿ (square), muthallath (triangle).
Some colours are named after things: burtuqālī (orange) comes from burtuqāl, the fruit, and bunnī (brown) comes from bunn, coffee beans.
stages.mnemonic: The colour follows the thing, like a shadow: boy aḥmar, girl ḥamrāʾ.
sentences: The ball is white and black.

gq.q: "Apple" (tuffāḥa) is feminine. Which phrase is right for "a red apple"?
gq.why: A feminine noun takes the feminine adjective ḥamrāʾ, and it comes after the noun.

gq.q: Where does the colour word go in an Arabic noun phrase?
o: At the end of the sentence
gq.why: Arabic adjectives follow the noun they describe.

panel.q: Why do we say "kitāb aḥmar" but "sayyāra ḥamrāʾ"?
o: Kitāb is masculine and sayyāra (car) is feminine
Cars are bigger than books, so the colour changes
Books are older than cars, so the colour is shorter
Colours change at night, so they need a new form
panel.why: Adjectives agree with the noun in gender.

panel.q: What do colour words like aḥmar, azraq and akhḍar share in form?
o: They follow the pattern aCCaC, with a feminine form CaCCāʾ
They all start with the letter b and end in -ī
They have no feminine form and never change
They are verbs that tell you what colour something becomes
panel.why: Arabic colour adjectives use the aCCaC pattern (masculine) and CaCCāʾ (feminine).

panel.q: Why does "the red car" have a different adjective ending from "the red book"?
panel.model: Because the adjective agrees with the noun in gender. Car (sayyāra) is feminine, so the adjective is ḥamrāʾ; book (kitāb) is masculine, so it is aḥmar.
panel.why: Gender agreement is required between noun and adjective.

teach.model: Colours are adjectives. They come after the noun and match its gender. For a boy word say aḥmar, for a girl word say ḥamrāʾ.

points.ask: What kind of word is red?
Where does it go?
Does the word change?

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: Who is in your family? Arabic has different words for "mum's brother" and "dad's brother". Why might a language be so careful?
explain: Basic family words are: umm (mother), ab (father), akh (brother), ukht (sister), jadd (grandfather), jadda (grandmother), walad (boy), bint (girl). Add "-ī" to mean "my": ummī, my mother.

Arabic is careful with relatives: ʿamm is a father's brother, khāl a mother's brother, ʿamma a father's sister, khāla a mother's sister. Family is very important in Arab cultures, and these words are used with love.
In speech, people also say mama and baba. These are dialect or child words, but they are used in almost every Arab country.
stages.mnemonic: "Ummī" = Mum + me. Add -ī and the word belongs to you.
sentences: My sister is in the house.

gq.why: Khāl is mother's brother; ʿamm is father's brother.

panel.q: Why does Arabic have separate words for uncles on each side?
o: Family ties are important and each relation has a clear place
Arabic lacks a general word for uncle, so it needed separate words
All uncles are the same, so the extra words are optional
The extra words only make spelling harder for children
panel.why: Arabic names the exact relationship, which fits the strong role of the extended family.

panel.q: What is the difference between "ummī" and "al-umm"?
o: Singular versus plural: one mother or several
panel.why: Ummī has the suffix "my"; al- is "the".

panel.q: A learner says "akh-ī" for "my sister". What is the problem?
o: Akh is brother; sister is ukht
Arabic has no word for sister
panel.why: The word is wrong, not the suffix. "My sister" is ukhtī.

teach.model: Mother is umm, father is ab, brother is akh and sister is ukht. Add -ī to say my. Arabic also has special words for uncles and aunts.

points.ask: How do I say mother and father?
How do I say my mother?
Are there other relatives?

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Point to the door, a pen and a chair. Which of these words in Arabic do you think is feminine? Look for a final -a!
explain: Common objects: ṭāwila (table), kursī (chair), bāb (door), nāfidha (window), qalam (pen), ḥaqība (bag), miftāḥ (key), kura (ball). Many nouns that end in -a (tāʾ marbūṭa ة) are feminine.

Put "al-" before a noun to say "the": al-bāb, the door. Before some letters the "l" is not said but the next letter is doubled: ash-shams (the sun), an-nāfidha (the window). These are called sun letters.
To say where something is, use prepositions: fī (in), ʿalā (on), taḥta (under). So al-qalam ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila means "the pen is on the table".
stages.mnemonic: Final ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) often means feminine: ṭāwila, nāfidha, ḥaqība.
sentences: The pen is on the table.
The key is in the bag.

gq.q: Which ending often shows a feminine noun?
gq.why: Nouns ending in ة, such as ḥaqība, are usually feminine.

panel.q: Why is "the sun" said ash-shams, not al-shams?
o: The "l" blends into sun letters and the next letter is doubled
It is a spelling mistake that readers have simply copied over time
Shams is a verb, so it takes a different article
Arabic has no L sound at the start of a word
panel.why: Sun letters absorb the l of al-, so we say ash-shams.

panel.q: Which phrase means "the key is under the table"?
panel.why: Taḥta means under, fī means in and ʿalā means on.

panel.q: A student says: "every noun ending in ة is feminine". What is the best reply?
o: Mostly true, but a few words for men, such as the name Usāma, end in ة
Never true, because ة is only a decoration mark
True for objects but false for people, with no exceptions at all
True without exception, because ة always marks feminine
panel.why: Final ة is a strong hint, not a rule: some masculine names end in it, and some feminine nouns (such as umm) do not.

teach.model: Arabic uses al- for the. The words fī, ʿalā and taḥta mean in, on and under. Many words that end in a taa marbuta are feminine.

points.ask: How do I say the?
How do I say where it is?
How can I guess a feminine word?

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: Mime eating, drinking, sleeping and reading. Which action word would you look up first in a dictionary?
explain: Arabic verbs have a root of usually three letters. The root k-t-b is about writing: yaktub (he writes), kātib (writer), kitāb (book), maktaba (library). The root stays; the pattern around it makes new words.

Present verbs begin with a letter showing who does the action: ya- (he), ta- (she or you), a- (I), na- (we). Examples: yaʾkul (he eats), yashrab (he drinks), yadhhab (he goes), yanām (he sleeps), yaqraʾ (he reads), yaktub (he writes), yalʿab (he plays), yarkuḍ (he runs).
In an Arabic dictionary, you look under the root. That is why knowing roots is one of the best tools for learning vocabulary.
stages.mnemonic: The root is a tree trunk: k-t-b grows book, writer, library.
sentences: The boy plays in the garden.

gq.q: Which letters make the root of kitāb, yaktub and kātib?
gq.why: The shared consonants k-t-b carry the idea of writing.

gq.q: Which prefix means "I" in a present verb?
gq.why: a- is "I", ya- is "he", ta- is "she/you", na- is "we".

panel.q: Why are roots useful for a learner?
o: One root links many words: kitāb, kātib, maktaba all share k-t-b
They are the same as vowels, so they only show sounds
They show the plural, so one root gives you every plural form
They give the pronunciation of every word you meet
panel.why: Seeing the same three consonants lets you guess the meaning of new words.

panel.q: Which sentence is correct for "she drinks tea"?
panel.why: For "she" the present begins with ta-.

panel.q: "Maktaba" means library. What do you expect "maktab" to relate to?
o: A place of writing, such as an office or desk
Eating or cooking, as in a kitchen or restaurant
A beach, a river or other place in nature
Sleep or rest, as in a bedroom or a bed
panel.why: The prefix ma- often gives a place noun, and the root is k-t-b: an office is a place where writing happens.

teach.model: Most Arabic words grow from a root of three letters, like k-t-b for writing. Present verbs begin with ya- for he, ta- for she, a- for I and na- for we.

points.ask: What is a root?
How does the verb show who does it?
Can you give an example?

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: Listen to a friend and say "I do not understand". What useful little phrases do you need to keep a talk going?
explain: Useful classroom phrases: naʿam (yes), lā (no), min faḍlika (please, to a man), min faḍliki (to a woman), āsif (sorry, said by a man; āsifa by a woman), lā afham (I do not understand), aʿid min faḍlik (say it again, please).
Arabic has different forms for "you" depending on who you talk to: -ka for a man and -ki for a woman. The two forms differ in one short vowel, so listen carefully.
Listening tip: read aloud with the harakat and copy the rhythm. Arabic has strong stress, long and short vowels, and often doubled consonants, shown with a mark called shadda.
stages.mnemonic: -ka for him, -ki for her: just one little vowel.
sentences: I do not understand the word.

gq.q: Which ending would you hear when talking politely to a woman: min faḍlika or min faḍliki?
gq.why: The feminine "you" ending is -ki; the masculine is -ka.

o: A long vowel, held twice as long
gq.why: Shadda marks a doubled sound, as in qiṭṭa (cat).

panel.q: A woman says "āsifa". What does this tell you?
o: The speaker is female: āsifa is the feminine form of sorry
The speaker is a child, because āsifa is a word used by children
The speaker is saying thanks in a polite and formal way
The speaker is asking a question about what to do next
panel.why: Adjective-like forms such as āsif / āsifa show the speaker's gender.

panel.q: Which phrase would you use to ask a teacher to say something again?
panel.why: "Aʿid" means "repeat".

panel.q: Why must a learner listen for the end of min faḍlika and min faḍliki?
panel.model: The final short vowel changes: -ka addresses a man, -ki a woman. Listening for it shows who is being addressed.
panel.why: The only difference between the masculine and feminine "you" is the final short vowel.

teach.model: Learn naʿam for yes and lā for no. Say min faḍlik for please. If you do not understand, say lā afham and aʿid min faḍlik. Use -ka for a man and -ki for a woman.

points.ask: How do I say yes and no?
What can I say if I do not understand?
How do I speak to a man or a woman?
